main.t: A curved plate of bone projecting into the nasal cavity from its lower side wall (inferior nasal concha).

simpler.t: The inferior nasal concha is a curved shelf of bone inside your nose.

deeper.t: Unlike the other two conchae, it is a separate bone, not part of the ethmoid.

facts.t: It projects from the lower part of each side wall of the nasal cavity.
The middle concha, part of the ethmoid, lies just above it.
It is paired: one on each side.

simpler.t: It sticks out from the side wall, low down inside your nose.

deeper.t: The tear drain (nasolacrimal duct) opens into the nasal cavity behind it.

items.name: Curved plate
items.t: Curves downwards as it projects into the nasal cavity.

items.name: Size
items.t: The largest of the three nasal conchae.

items.name: Attached edge
items.t: Fixed to the lower part of the side wall of the nasal cavity.

items.name: Visible from the front
items.t: It can easily be seen looking into the front opening of the nasal cavity.

simpler.t: It is a curved shelf, the biggest of three on each side of the nose.

deeper.t: The conchae are named for their positions: superior, middle and inferior.

facts.t: Its downward curve swirls incoming air, helping to warm and moisten it before it reaches the lungs.
Mucus on its lining traps dust, pollen, bacteria and viruses.

simpler.t: It stirs the air you breathe, so the air is warmed, moistened and cleaned.

items.name: Middle nasal concha
items.t: Part of the ethmoid bone, just above it.

items.name: Ethmoid bone
items.t: Forms the superior and middle conchae.

items.name: Nasolacrimal duct
items.t: Opens into the nasal cavity behind it.

items.name: Nasal cavity
items.t: It projects into the lower part of each side.

simpler.t: It sits below the ethmoid’s conchae, with the tear drain opening behind it.

facts.t: The inferior concha forms from a cartilage model (endochondral ossification).
facts.check: OpenStax 7.5 says the facial bones form from cartilage; that this applies to the inferior nasal concha needs an approved source.

items.damaged: Nothing is damaged: the tear drain behind the inferior concha is overloaded.
items.why: Extra tears entering the nasal cavity behind the concha also drain forwards.

items.damaged: The lining over the conchae swells.
items.why: The swollen lining narrows the air passages around the conchae.
items.check: Swelling of the lining narrowing the nasal passages is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.q: Explain how the nasal conchae prepare the air you breathe.
model: They are curved plates projecting into the nasal cavity.
This helps warm and moisten it.
Mucus on them traps dust, pollen, bacteria and viruses.

items.q: Compare the inferior nasal concha with the middle and superior conchae.
model: The inferior concha is a separate bone; the other two are part of the ethmoid.
It is the largest; the superior is the smallest.
The inferior and middle conchae can be seen from the front.
The superior concha is hidden above and behind the middle one.

items.q: Predict what happens to dust you breathe in through your nose.
model: The conchae swirl the incoming air.
Dust meets the mucus on their lining.
So cleaner, warmer, moister air moves on towards the lungs.

check.stem: Which nasal concha is a separate bone?
check.why: The inferior nasal concha is an independent bone of the skull.

check.stem: Which is the largest nasal concha?
check.why: The inferior concha is the largest.

check.stem: What do the nasal conchae do to incoming air?
options: Swirl it, so it is warmed and moistened
check.why: They swirl the air, which helps warm and moisturise it.
